segments.text: This review asks why two surveys can report different galaxy metallicities before the galaxies themselves differ. It separates three effects that are often mixed together: calibration scale, aperture, and diffuse ionized gas.

Theoretical photoionization calibrations and empirical electron-temperature calibrations can differ by roughly 0.7 dex in absolute oxygen abundance. That is about a factor of five before any physical evolution is inferred.

Below about twenty percent covering fraction, a fixed fiber can bias metallicity by more than 0.15 dex. Central regions are typically richer, so the aperture can manufacture mass trends and even a false turnover.

Diffuse ionized gas can supply thirty to sixty percent of H-alpha emission. Its harder spectrum boosts low-ionization line ratios, which can flatten or even invert the metallicity gradients inferred from integrated light.

Use one declared abundance scale with published conversions. Enforce covering-fraction floors or calibrated aperture corrections. Then use integral-field spectroscopy as the independent ground truth for the integrated relation.

The contribution is this framework, not a new metallicity measurement. The thresholds come from published literature. Automated review-cleared status is a workflow gate, not human or journal peer review. The draft is not validated.
